items.stimulus:
Microplastics are usually defined as plastic fragments smaller than five millimetres. Some are manufactured at that size, such as the abrasive beads once common in facial scrubs, but most of those found in fresh water are thought to come from the breakdown of larger items: bottles and bags weathered by sunlight, fibres shed from synthetic clothing in washing machines, and particles worn from vehicle tyres and washed off roads by rain. Because research on plastic pollution began in the oceans, rivers and lakes received comparatively little attention until the 2010s. Freshwater systems are now recognised not only as polluted environments in their own right but as the main routes by which plastic from the land reaches the sea.

Measuring how much plastic a river carries is harder than it sounds. Samples are typically collected with fine nets towed near the surface, so the result depends heavily on mesh size: a net with openings of about a third of a millimetre lets through every particle smaller than that, and the smallest fragments are often the most numerous. Concentrations also vary with the weather. After heavy rain, runoff from streets and overflowing sewers can raise counts many times over within hours, so a single sample may say little about typical conditions. For these reasons, figures from different studies are difficult to compare directly.

Wastewater treatment plants play an ambiguous role. Modern plants remove a large majority of incoming microplastics, but the particles they capture end up in sewage sludge, which in many countries is spread on farmland as fertiliser. From there, some may be washed back into streams. Lakes add a further complication: because water moves slowly through them, they can act as traps where particles settle into the bottom sediments, which some researchers now treat as a record of how pollution has changed over decades.

The effects on freshwater life remain uncertain. Laboratory studies have shown that small invertebrates and fish readily swallow microplastics, sometimes eating less food as a result, but many experiments used concentrations far higher than those found in most rivers. Whether present-day levels cause measurable harm in the wild is still being investigated.

items.stimulus:
A nudge is a change in the way choices are presented that makes one option more likely to be chosen without forbidding any alternative or significantly changing its cost. The idea was popularised by the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein in a book published in 2008, and within a few years several governments had set up units to apply it, the first being a team created within the British Cabinet Office in 2010.

The most studied nudge is the default. When employees are enrolled in a workplace pension automatically and must actively opt out if they do not want it, participation is typically far higher than when they must actively sign up, even though the choice open to them is identical. Other nudges rely on social comparison, such as a letter telling a household that its electricity use is above that of similar homes nearby, or on simple timing, such as a text message reminding a patient of an appointment the day before.

Supporters argue that nudges are cheap, preserve freedom of choice and work with, rather than against, the way people actually make decisions. Critics raise two broad objections. The first concerns effectiveness: early studies often reported impressive results, but later reviews that gathered larger numbers of trials, including unpublished ones, found that the average effect was considerably smaller, and that some well-known findings could not be repeated. The second objection is ethical. Because nudges often work best when people do not notice them, some argue that they bypass reasoning and are therefore a subtle form of manipulation, particularly when the government decides which option is in a person's interest.

Defenders reply that every choice must be presented in some way, so there is no neutral option: a form must list its boxes in some order, and a default must be either one thing or another. On this view, the real question is not whether to influence choices but whether the influence is transparent and could be justified openly to the people affected.

items.stimulus:
The arrangement of letters on most English-language keyboards takes its name from the first six letters of the top row. It was developed in the 1870s by the American inventor Christopher Latham Sholes and his collaborators, and reached the market on a typewriter manufactured by the firm of E. Remington and Sons from 1874. A popular explanation holds that the layout was designed to slow typists down. A more careful version of the story is that early typewriters jammed when the metal arms carrying neighbouring letters were struck in quick succession, so Sholes separated some letters that often appear together. Even this account is disputed: some historians argue that the layout was shaped largely by the requests of telegraph operators, who were among the machine's first customers.

Whatever its origins, the layout outlived the mechanical problem it may have been meant to solve. In 1936 the educational psychologist August Dvorak patented an alternative that placed the most frequently used letters on the middle row, and enthusiasts long claimed that it allowed much faster typing. In 1985 the economist Paul David used QWERTY as a leading example of what he called path dependence: once enough typists had been trained on one layout and enough machines built for it, switching became costly for everyone, even if a better design existed. Each typist had little reason to learn a layout that few employers used, and employers had little reason to buy machines that few typists could operate.

Not all economists accepted this story. In 1990 two of them reviewed the evidence for Dvorak's superiority and concluded that much of it came from studies of poor quality, some conducted by Dvorak himself, and that a later government trial had found no meaningful advantage. If the alternative was not clearly better, they argued, the survival of QWERTY shows little about markets failing to adopt superior technology. The debate continues partly because the question is hard to test: typists who learn a new layout as adults bring years of habit with them, and people trained from the start on Dvorak's layout are relatively rare.
items.question: Sholes himself intended the QWERTY layout to make typists work more slowly.

For much of the twentieth century, most consumer goods were sold once: a customer paid for a record, a piece of software or a car, and the transaction was complete. Over the past two decades, a growing range of products has moved to a subscription model, in which customers pay a regular fee for continued access. Music, films, software, news, meal kits and even some car features can now be paid for by the month.

For firms, the attraction is predictability. A business that sells one-off products must find new buyers every quarter, whereas one with subscribers begins each month with revenue it can largely forecast. Investors tend to value such recurring income highly, which encourages companies to convert existing products.

The economics of the model rest on two figures: the cost of acquiring a subscriber and the rate at which subscribers cancel, usually called churn. A service that spends heavily on advertising and introductory discounts can only recover that spending if customers stay long enough. A monthly churn rate of five per cent may sound modest, but it means that the average subscriber stays for only about twenty months, and a firm must recruit new customers equal to more than half its customer base each year simply to stand still.

For consumers, the picture is more mixed. Subscriptions lower the upfront price and can give access to far larger catalogues than most people could afford to buy outright. Yet they also turn ownership into a continuing obligation, and many people underestimate how much they spend because small monthly fees are easy to forget. Some firms appear to rely on this inattention, making sign-up effortless and cancellation laborious. It seems to me that this asymmetry, rather than the subscription itself, is the real problem. A subscription that customers can leave as easily as they joined is a fair bargain that must keep earning their loyalty; one designed to be hard to leave profits from friction rather than from value. Rules requiring cancellation to be as simple as sign-up would do more for consumers than attempts to discourage subscriptions altogether.

items.stimulus:
When speakers of one language adopt a word from another, linguists call the result a loanword, although nothing is ever given back. Borrowing is one of the most common ways in which vocabularies grow, and few languages are untouched by it. English is an extreme case: after the Norman Conquest of 1066, French became a principal language of the court, the law and government in England for several centuries, and thousands of French words entered English, many of them in exactly those fields.

Borrowed words rarely arrive unchanged. They are usually reshaped to fit the sound system of the language that receives them. Japanese, which generally does not allow two consonants together or most consonants at the end of a word, inserts vowels, so that the English 'Christmas' becomes 'kurisumasu'. Meanings shift too. The English word 'mansion' entered Japanese as 'manshon', but there it usually refers to a block of flats rather than a grand house. Over time, a well-established loanword may be treated by speakers as entirely native, its foreign origin known only to those who look it up.

Not every borrowing involves the sounds of the original. In a loan translation, or calque, a language copies the structure of a foreign word using its own parts. German 'Wolkenkratzer' and French 'gratte-ciel' both render the idea of the English 'skyscraper' in native elements, meaning roughly 'cloud-scraper' and 'scrape-sky'.

Attitudes to borrowing vary widely. Icelandic has a long tradition of creating new words from native roots rather than adopting foreign ones; its word for computer combines older words for 'number' and 'prophetess'. In France, official commissions publish recommended French terms for new technologies, though speakers do not always use them. Such efforts show that borrowing is not simply automatic. Yet they also suggest that it cannot be fully controlled, since the words people actually use are settled in everyday speech rather than by decree.

Civil disobedience is usually defined as a deliberate and public breach of the law, undertaken to change a law or policy that the person believes to be seriously unjust. The definition already distinguishes it from ordinary crime. A thief hopes not to be noticed and gains personally from the act; a civil disobedient wants the breach to be seen, and the aim is to persuade the wider community rather than to benefit privately.

Philosophers who defend the practice in a democracy usually attach conditions to it. The first is that lawful channels, such as petitions, elections and the courts, should normally have been tried first, or be clearly unavailable. The second is that the protest should avoid harming others; a sit-in that blocks the entrance to a building for an afternoon is quite different from damaging property or endangering lives. The third, and the most debated, is that protesters should openly accept the legal penalty. Accepting punishment, defenders say, shows respect for the legal system as a whole even while one part of it is being challenged, and demonstrates that the protester is sincere rather than merely seeking advantage.

Critics question each of these conditions. Waiting for lawful channels may take years, during which the injustice continues; for those directly affected, the demand for patience can itself seem unjust. The requirement to accept punishment has also been challenged. items.stimulus:
Before 1840, sending a letter within Britain was expensive and complicated. Charges depended on the distance travelled and the number of sheets of paper, and the cost was normally paid by the person receiving the letter rather than the sender. Recipients could refuse a letter, leaving the Post Office with the expense of carrying it for nothing, and some correspondents exploited the system by marking the outside of a letter with coded signs so that the recipient could read the message without accepting it. Members of Parliament, meanwhile, were entitled to send mail free of charge, a privilege that was widely abused.

In 1837 Rowland Hill, a schoolmaster and reformer, published a pamphlet arguing that the real cost of carrying a letter lay mostly in handling, not in distance. He proposed a single low rate for letters throughout the country, paid in advance by the sender. Lower prices, he predicted, would increase the volume of mail so much that revenue would eventually recover. After a public campaign, a uniform rate of one penny for a letter weighing up to half an ounce was introduced on 10 January 1840. The adhesive stamp that would show prepayment, later known as the Penny Black, was issued on 1 May and could be used from 6 May.

The stamp carried a profile of the young Queen Victoria and, unusually by later standards, no name of the country, a convention that British stamps still follow. Each sheet contained 240 stamps, worth exactly one pound, and letters printed in the lower corners of each stamp identified its position on the sheet, making forgery harder.

The design had a weakness. Used stamps were cancelled with red ink, which was difficult to see on the black background and could be removed, so that stamps might be cleaned and used again. In 1841 the colour of the penny stamp was changed to red and cancellations were made in black.

Hill's reform transformed communication. The number of letters more than doubled in the first year and continued to grow. His financial forecast proved less accurate: the Post Office's net income fell sharply and took many years to return to its earlier level.

items.stimulus:
The word triage comes from a French verb meaning to sort, and the practice is often traced to military surgeons of the Napoleonic era, who began treating wounded soldiers according to the seriousness of their injuries rather than their rank. Today it is a routine part of every large emergency department, where the number of patients arriving at any moment may far exceed the staff available to see them.

In Australian and New Zealand emergency departments, patients are usually assessed on arrival by an experienced nurse using the Australasian Triage Scale. This assigns each person to one of five categories, each linked to the maximum time the patient should wait before being assessed and treated by a clinician. Category 1 patients, whose lives are under immediate threat, should be seen at once; category 2 within ten minutes; category 3 within half an hour; category 4 within an hour; and category 5 within two hours. Similar five-level systems are used elsewhere, including the United Kingdom.

Triage is not diagnosis. The assessment typically takes only a few minutes and relies on the main complaint, a brief history and basic observations such as pulse, breathing rate and level of consciousness. Its purpose is to answer a narrower question: how long can this person safely wait? A patient with a broken wrist may be in great pain yet be safe to wait longer than a quiet patient whose breathing rate is steadily rising. For this reason the order in which people are seen can appear unfair to those in the waiting room, who see others called before them despite having arrived later.

Errors occur in both directions. Under-triage, placing a patient in a less urgent category than needed, risks delayed treatment of a serious condition. Over-triage uses scarce resources on patients who could have waited. Because the first is usually more dangerous, nurses are often encouraged to choose the more urgent category when in doubt, and patients are reassessed if their condition changes while they wait.

In my view, the most important feature of a triage system is not its exact categories but its consistency. A scale is only useful if two nurses assessing the same patient would place that patient in the same category, which is why departments audit triage decisions and train staff to apply the criteria in the same way.

items.stimulus:
The word triage comes from a French verb meaning to sort, and the practice is often traced to military surgeons of the Napoleonic era, who began treating wounded soldiers according to the seriousness of their injuries rather than their rank. Today it is a routine part of every large emergency department, where the number of patients arriving at any moment may far exceed the staff available to see them.

In Australian and New Zealand emergency departments, patients are usually assessed on arrival by an experienced nurse using the Australasian Triage Scale. This assigns each person to one of five categories, each linked to the maximum time the patient should wait before being assessed and treated by a clinician. Category 1 patients, whose lives are under immediate threat, should be seen at once; category 2 within ten minutes; category 3 within half an hour; category 4 within an hour; and category 5 within two hours. Similar five-level systems are used elsewhere, including the United Kingdom.

Triage is not diagnosis. The assessment typically takes only a few minutes and relies on the main complaint, a brief history and basic observations such as pulse, breathing rate and level of consciousness. Its purpose is to answer a narrower question: how long can this person safely wait? A patient with a broken wrist may be in great pain yet be safe to wait longer than a quiet patient whose breathing rate is steadily rising. For this reason the order in which people are seen can appear unfair to those in the waiting room, who see others called before them despite having arrived later.

Errors occur in both directions. Under-triage, placing a patient in a less urgent category than needed, risks delayed treatment of a serious condition. Over-triage uses scarce resources on patients who could have waited. Because the first is usually more dangerous, nurses are often encouraged to choose the more urgent category when in doubt, and patients are reassessed if their condition changes while they wait.

In my view, the most important feature of a triage system is not its exact categories but its consistency. A scale is only useful if two nurses assessing the same patient would place that patient in the same category, which is why departments audit triage decisions and train staff to apply the criteria in the same way.

Connoisseurship remains important, but its limits were exposed in the twentieth century. In the 1930s and 1940s the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren produced a series of pictures in the style of Johannes Vermeer that were accepted by leading specialists and bought by wealthy collectors and a museum. He was exposed only after the Second World War, when he was accused of having sold a national treasure to a senior Nazi and chose to prove that the painting was his own work. To show that he could do it, he painted a further 'Vermeer' while under supervision.

Scientific methods now support the expert's judgement. X-ray images can reveal earlier compositions hidden under the visible surface, which may show that a canvas was reused or that the artist changed his mind in ways typical of genuine work. Analysis of pigments can expose anachronisms: a white pigment based on titanium, for example, was not widely available to artists until the twentieth century, so its presence in a supposed seventeenth-century picture is decisive evidence against it. Wooden panels can sometimes be dated from the pattern of their growth rings.

A skilled forger who uses old materials, such as a period canvas with its original picture scraped off, may pass every laboratory test. items.stimulus:
Copyright gives creators the exclusive right to copy and distribute their work, but in almost every legal system that right is temporary. When it expires, the work enters the public domain, where anyone may reprint, adapt or perform it without permission or payment. The length of protection has grown steadily. Britain's first copyright statute, passed in 1710, protected books for fourteen years, with a possible second term of fourteen years if the author was still alive. Today the standard term in Australia, the European Union and the United States is the life of the author plus seventy years, so a work written by a young author who lives a long life may remain protected for well over a century.

The usual justification for copyright is that it encourages creation: without some period of exclusive rights, authors and publishers could not recover the cost of producing new work. That argument explains why copyright should exist, but it is much weaker as a defence of very long terms. An author deciding whether to write a novel is unlikely to be influenced by income that will arrive decades after his or her death, and extending the term of works that already exist cannot encourage their creation, since they have already been made. Yet several extensions have applied to existing works as well as new ones.

The costs of long terms fall largely on the public domain. Most works stop earning money long before their protection ends, but because tracing the owners of old rights can be difficult or impossible, many such works cannot legally be reissued, digitised or adapted. Libraries and archives hold large numbers of these so-called orphan works.

I do not argue that copyright should be abolished; creators deserve to be paid, and a reasonable period of protection serves that end. But the balance has tipped too far. A term long enough to reward authors during their working lives, with some provision for their families, would protect the incentive to create while returning culture to common use within a lifetime rather than after several.

The browning of a seared steak, a slice of toast or roasted coffee beans is largely the work of the Maillard reaction, named after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912. It is not a single reaction but a network of many, beginning when an amino acid, one of the building blocks of proteins, reacts with certain sugars. The products break down and recombine into hundreds of different compounds, some of which give roasted and baked foods their characteristic aromas, while others form brown pigments.

The Maillard reaction is often confused with caramelisation, which also produces brown colour and rich flavour. Caramelisation, however, involves sugars alone and generally needs higher temperatures.
